newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Franco-Dutch drugs rift may sour Hague presidency.
newsitem.headline: Franco-Dutch drugs rift may sour Hague presidency.

text.p: As the Netherlands prepares to take over the presidency of the European Union in three weeks, there are growing fears that a row over its liberal drugs policy could hamper progress on weightier issues facing the 15-member bloc.

Fresh attacks by French President Jacques Chirac on the eve of Friday's European Union summit in Dublin have further isolated the Dutch stance on drugs and the issue is unlikely to go away during the Hague's six-month presidency.

"There is a fear here that the drugs issue, which we think is minor, could damage progress on the IGC (inter-governmental conference review of EU treaties) and EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) during our presidency," one Dutch ministerial aide said.

Dutch officials had hoped that agreement on a common European policy against drugs, thrashed out in Brussels last month, had taken the heat out of an issue which has driven a wedge between the Netherlands and its 14 EU partners.

Under the compromise deal, EU members will unite to fight drug trafficking and addiction, but can "maintain or introduce more efficient measures" to control drugs, leaving the Dutch free to continue a progressive 20-year experiment in allowing the small-scale sale and use of soft drugs, such as cannabis.

Drugs are illegal in the Netherlands, but sales of modest amounts of soft drugs from over 1,200 "coffee-shops" are allowed in the belief that decriminalising their use keeps youngsters out of the clutches of underworld hard-drug "pushers".
The Dutch defend their policy with statistics that show fewer drug addicts, HIV-infections and drug-related deaths than in other European countries.
But seasoned observers of the Franco-Dutch drugs rift warned that the text left the way open for fresh wrangling.

"Make no mistake, the accord... does not mean an end to this drugs affair," former European Commissioner Frans Andriessen warned in a newspaper commentary, adding that Chirac had made drugs, and in particular Dutch laxity, a crusading issue.
"Chirac has not yet approved the...text. He will undoubtedly raise the issue at the (Dublin) summit and maybe again later."

France protests that Dutch policy attracts drug "tourists" -- youngsters who visit the Netherlands to buy cheap and readily available narcotics -- and Chirac continued his broadside this week, insisting The Hague fall in line with the rest of Europe.

"There is one country, Holland, which has totally different legislation. That is why I think an effort must be made to harmonise legislation, for the health of our young people, and for the spirit of Europe itself..," he said on Monday.
Publicly, the Dutch say they have not heard officially from Paris and do not expect drugs to be an issue at Dublin.
But there is private dismay at the prospect that their presidency -- aimed at promoting European unity -- could be bogged down in endless rows over how to combat the drug threat.
"We all want the same thing, but we have our own way of going about it," one Dutch diplomat commented.
The French and Dutch have engaged in a long-running war of words over Dutch policy, which escalated sharply last March after a French official dubbed the Netherlands a "narco-state".
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok called Chirac "unbalanced" on the issue, and the Dutch media have hinted at drug-related problems within the French leader's own family.
Dutch European Commissioner Hans van den Broek has also told the Hague to review its "ideological pet" to see if it could achieve fewer drug-related deaths and addiction by other means.
He said the Dutch could not stand in isolation and must appreciate that its policy caused problems for its neighbours.
"The limits of your tolerant policy stop where it begins to be a nuisance to others," he said.
